title: How To Break One Bad Habit And Improve Every Area Of Classroom Management very-area-of-classroom-management/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: After watching many teachers in action, Linsin identifies a single common bad habit among those who struggle with management: they take their eyes off their students for long stretches while engrossed in instruction or other tasks, often without realizing it. He walks through six benefits of staying visually vigilant — consistency, having firsthand truth when enforcing consequences, avoiding arguments, building trust, projecting presence, and earning respect — arguing each stems directly from actually seeing misbehavior occur. He acknowledges teachers can't catch everything but insists vigilance is a learnable skill built through smart positioning, active peripheral vision, and strict verification of expectations. Practical tips include pulling individual students to the room's edge rather than losing sight of the group, and relying on frequent unpredictable glances during small-group rotations.
points: The most common bad habit among struggling teachers is simply taking their eyes off the class for long stretches without realizing it.
Personally witnessing misbehavior gives a teacher "truth" — proof that lets them enforce consequences swiftly without arguments.
Being visibly observant builds trust, because students feel protected from disruption when they know the teacher misses very little.
Vigilance is a learnable skill: use smart positioning, active peripheral vision, and frequent unpredictable glances during group work.
When helping an individual student, position them at the room's edge rather than losing sight of the rest of the class.
quotes: If we were to place a video camera in their classroom, their jaw would drop at the misbehavior going on right underneath their nose.
You can’t be consistent if you don’t see when your students misbehave. And inconsistency equals increased misbehavior every time.
When you personally witness misbehavior, you have truth on your side. You have the only proof you need to swiftly and calmly follow your classroom management plan.
There is something about breaking rules within the full view of a respected, well-liked teacher that makes students very uncomfortable.
The key is smart positioning, active peripheral vision, and the shrewd insistence on verifying every expectation you set for your students.
At all times, however, you must stay in the moment. Keep your students in front of you.
